note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Follow a whole flowering stem to its widely spreading, fine, often slightly stiff panicle branches. Kew describes an open panicle approximately 25–45 cm long and 15–30 cm wide. Spikelets are carried separately on slender stalks, not bunched into dense groups. Fresh purple is a helpful memory cue but turns tan and is never decisive alone.
tiles.short: A broad, airy panicle with small separated spikelets
tiles.status: REAL GROSS FLOWERING STRUCTURES PRESENT; SAME-PLANT SCALE GAP

tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE PERENNIAL CROWN
tiles.details: A warm-season perennial tuft with short knotty rhizomes, usually roughly 40–75 cm culms and 3–7 mm blades in Kew's treatment. Mature flowering panicles may break away as tumbleweeds; a loose dried head without its original crown cannot prove growth form. Gallery panels 3–4 (zero-based indices) now show actual basal blades and a ground-anchored leafy tuft, but neither exposes roots or short knotty rhizomes; no single locally vouchered crown-to-spikelet sequence is documented.
tiles.short: Short knotty rhizomes and mostly basal leaves
tiles.status: PUBLISHED GROWTH FORM; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CONNECTED ROOTED CROWN

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS AND MEASURE GLUMES
tiles.details: Under a 10–20× lens, measure an intact laterally compressed spikelet: Kew gives about 5–7 mm by 1.5–2 mm and 7–11 fertile florets; broader regional accounts include about 3–7.5 mm and 4–12 florets. Two short basal one-veined glumes are roughly 1–2.3 mm in Go Botany. These figures come from botanical treatments, not measured pixels in the current gallery photographs.
tiles.short: Usually 5–7 mm spikelets, 7–11 florets in Kew
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CALIBRATED MATURE SPIKELET AND TWO GLUMES

tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK THE LEMMA, PALEA AND AWNS
tiles.details: Separate one mature floret. Regional descriptions give three-veined fertile lemmas about 1.4–2.5 mm and paleas around 1–2.4 mm; the florets have no projecting awns. Photograph the actual lemma dorsal veins, palea and floret attachment beside a millimeter scale. Do not place a glume or lemma arrow on the existing wide panicle photographs.
tiles.short: Three-veined, roughly 1.4–2.5 mm lemmas; no long awns

tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE COLLAR, NOT A STEM NODE
tiles.details: Inspect the blade–sheath junction at 10–30×. Kew describes the ligule as a FRINGE OF HAIRS; regional keys may describe a minute ciliate membranous base (~0.2–0.4 mm), while conspicuous oral/sheath-throat hairs can be several millimeters long. Do not measure those long sheath hairs as the tiny membrane. Document both separately with a 1-mm scale; published descriptions differ in how the hair fringe and membrane are characterized. The two NEW source-authenticated, public-site-compatible panels show only the OUTER white collar hair tuft and the V-shaped blade-sheath insertion; neither is a measured peeled-open inner true ligule. Their arrows do not identify a tiny unproven ligule. Panel 7 (zero-based) also shows actual long OUTER sheath-mouth hairs; it does not reveal the minute free inner ligule.
tiles.short: Very short true ligule region beside longer sheath-throat hairs
tiles.status: OUTER COLLAR/SHEATH PHOTOGRAPHED — INNER TRUE LIGULE MACRO NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO

tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE RED LOVEGRASS AND WITCHGRASS
tiles.details: E. secundiflora tends to have denser groups of larger spikelets on shorter ascending branches; E. intermedia and E. trichodes can also be airy and require sheath and mature spikelet checks. Panicum capillare and Digitaria cognata can make a tumbleweed-like cloud but have fundamentally different spikelet/floret architecture. The existing E. secundiflora panel is explicitly DIFFERENT SPECIES; verify same-angle local photographs before a finished comparison. The true red-lovegrass comparison is panel 9 (zero-based); panels 0 and 2 are purple-lovegrass architecture, not look-alike images.
tiles.short: Widely spaced many-flowered spikelets, not clustered or one-flowered
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MATCHED LOCAL COMPARISON

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Start with the broad, loose, cloudlike PANICLE on a basal clump. Follow individual long, spreading, flexible branches and note the small spikelets spaced apart. A mature head can detach and tumble. Purple color is only a supporting cue, not the ID; compare panicle BRANCHING and spikelet clustering with E. secundiflora.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with nine exact-species gallery panels: flowering heads (0–2), basal leafy tuft (3–4), external sheath/collar views (5–7), and a genuine flower macro (8). The tenth panel (9) is DIFFERENT SPECIES, E. secundiflora. The grounded crown does not expose roots or rhizomes; the flower macro does not resolve measured glumes/lemmas.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Inspect the blade–sheath junction at 10–30×. Kew describes the ligule as a FRINGE OF HAIRS; regional keys may describe a minute ciliate membranous base (~0.2–0.4 mm), while conspicuous oral/sheath-throat hairs can be several millimeters long. Do not measure those long sheath hairs as the tiny membrane. Document both separately with a 1-mm scale; published descriptions differ in how the hair fringe and membrane are characterized. The two NEW source-authenticated, public-site-compatible panels show only the OUTER white collar hair tuft and the V-shaped blade-sheath insertion; neither is a measured peeled-open inner true ligule. Their arrows do not identify a tiny unproven ligule. Panel 7 (zero-based) also shows actual long OUTER sheath-mouth hairs; it does not reveal the minute free inner ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Under a 10–20× lens, measure an intact laterally compressed spikelet: Kew gives about 5–7 mm by 1.5–2 mm and 7–11 fertile florets; broader regional accounts include about 3–7.5 mm and 4–12 florets. Two short basal one-veined glumes are roughly 1–2.3 mm in Go Botany. These figures come from botanical treatments, not measured pixels in the current gallery photographs.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: E. secundiflora: comparatively chunky panicle, much larger many-flowered spikelets clumped along shorter ascending branches. E. intermedia and E. trichodes: also airy; sheath-throat and mature spikelet details needed. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) may resemble a fine cloud but has different reproductive spikelet structure.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 1 · Fine spread of flowering branches
panels.caption: This verified local JPEG shows the fine, open flowering branches above green leaves and a basal leafy crown. Arrows point to visible coarse structures only; the roots, true ligule and measured spikelets are not resolved.
panels.creator: David J. Stang
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: 3 · PURPLE LOVEGRASS — archived open-panicle variation
panels.caption: Another true purple lovegrass photograph showing how loose flowering heads can overlap and vary in shape. Learn the branching architecture, but never claim individual spikelet nerves or a hair-fringed ligule from this view.
panels.creator: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: BASAL LEAF DETAILS · same-species photographed lower tuft
panels.caption: Real photographed low leafy crown of source-labelled purple lovegrass. The dark upright reddish blade and cluster of basal leaf blades are visible. Root attachment, isolated ligule, 0.2–0.4 mm fringe/membrane and spikelets cannot be resolved. Original David J. Stang photograph, CC BY-SA 4.0.
panels.creator: David J. Stang
panels.modifications: Resaved at source dimensions with EXIF/GPS removed; no crop

panels.label: GROWING IN SOIL · ground-anchored leafy crown (roots not exposed)
panels.caption: David J. Stang's photographed living Eragrostis spectabilis at the United States Botanic Garden. The green crown and many narrow leaves visibly emerge from soil. This helps crew recognize a low tuft in the ground, but does NOT demonstrate an excavated knotty rhizome, emerging subterranean node, 0.1–0.4 mm true ligule or attached full seedhead. The botanical-garden plant is not a local Hays County voucher.
panels.creator: David J. Stang

intro: Start with the broad, loose, cloudlike PANICLE on a basal clump. Follow individual long, spreading, flexible branches and note the small spikelets spaced apart. memory_rule: BROAD OPEN TUMBLING CLOUD with individual spikelets spaced along fine spreading branches; purple is optional.
safety_note: Nine exact-species teaching panels and one E. secundiflora comparison are recorded; verify each archived file, image-level rights and public rendering. Only gross-structure arrows currently justified; no licensed true-collar or isolated-scale spikelet closeup added in this pass. Minnesota Wildflowers morphology macro and university photo sources are reference-only without established image redistribution permissions. Added one CC BY-SA 4.0 lower-tuft image showing REAL basal blades (not exposed ligule); true collar/spikelet/glume/lemma photos remain essential. 2026-10-26: added real source-authenticated 1000x667 in-ground basal tuft (David J. Stang, CC BY-SA 4.0) with two crown/blade arrows; crown is soil-anchored, actual rhizomes and roots remain hidden. Complete attached flowering-head images are preserved separately. October 26: added TWO individually licensed Research Grade photographic collar/sheath panels with four gross arrows. One NC image is only conditionally usable on this genuinely noncommercial learner. Neither reveals true measured inner ligule; keep this photo hold. 2026-10-26 Anne Parker CC BY Research Grade external hairy blade-base macro physically stored, one gross hair-arrow, YES outer hairs, NO peeled true ligule or calibrated micromorphology. Strict completion remains blocked. 2026-10-26 exact-source actual ligule and collar photographs discovered on Missouri State's purple-lovegrass page, but author requires express permission for one-time web reuse; NOT installed, NO measured scale, remaining strict photo hold. See reports/lane2-purple-lovegrass-true-ligule-permission-lead-20261026.json.
field_rule: Wide transparent open panicle + spaced small many-flowered awnless spikelets + extremely short ciliate ligule set apart from 2–4 mm sheath-apex hairs; confirm fine anatomy at scale.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
